entry.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen
entry.content:
Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen

Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen, bringing cutting-edge intelligence to everyone — with speed and efficiency for everyday coding and agentic workflows.

While our frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, excel at deep, long-horizon reasoning on your hardest problems, Hydrogen is built for rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows. With Hydrogen, we’re also bringing Gemini 4 to everyone — for all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for business, the Gemini app, Google Search, and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity.

Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is priced flat across its entire 1 million-token context window at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads

In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.

To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.

Scaling developer and enterprise workflows

Beyond multi-model workflows, Hydrogen is a major standalone upgrade for teams migrating from Gemini 3.8 Flash. It delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence — finishing tasks 2.5 times faster at its high default setting while more than tripling Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores (57% vs. 18.2%), cutting fabricated claims by more than 5x, and adapting cleanly when a tool call fails or a search returns empty. It also matches or outperforms competing models in its class across core developer and enterprise workflows:

Iterative repository coding and debugging: Hydrogen handles issue resolution, debugging, rapid iteration, and codebase Q&A with focused, surgical edits — delivering cleaner, production-ready code without rewriting unrelated files. It outperforms similar-tier models on SWE-sweep where it has to discover and repair bugs without breaking existing code. To explore large repositories efficiently, the model excels at natively batching file-read and search calls in parallel rather than inspecting files one by one; in early testing across complex graphs, SQL, and data-heavy enterprise workflows, our partners have seen Hydrogen run 2x to 2.8x faster while reducing token usage by 12% to 23%, compared to 3.8 Flash. Open-ended agentic execution: On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks #5 on Agent Arena, arena.ai’s live benchmark. For deep domain reasoning and analysis, it leads its class on HLE-Diamond (58.8%), ranks #1 overall on Vals Tax Agent Bench (52.3%), ties for #1 on the Vals Legal Research Bench (55.8%), and leads its class on AutomationBench-AA. Multimodal knowledge work: Hydrogen pairs native 1 million-token input with up to 1 million output tokens to synthesize dense PDFs, spreadsheets, charts, audio, and recorded video into polished, cited reports and structured deliverables. It outperforms other models on the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark (53.4%) for end-to-end agentic knowledge work over complex visual files, and on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 (71.6%) for end-to-end professional workflows. Web development: On tasks where speed matters to developers, like live UI prototyping, design-to-code iteration, and interactive app building, Hydrogen generates more functional, feature-complete layouts in fewer prompts. Adaptable speed and intelligence across four thinking levels

We built Gemini 4 Hydrogen for real-world usability. Hydrogen’s four thinking levels — low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier — offer a wide range of options across quality, latency, and cost, scaling in a smooth, predictable progression so you only wait and pay for the reasoning depth a task requires. Across thinking levels, Hydrogen matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class while often finishing tasks faster and using fewer output tokens.

Fast, everyday help in the Gemini app and Search

For consumers, Gemini 4 Hydrogen makes it easier to get things done, staying on track and following instructions more closely across multi-turn conversations.

In the Gemini app, Hydrogen makes your everyday assistant even more helpful — it’s better at following your guidance, calling the right tools, and getting you to a reliable output with less back-and-forth.

Ready-to-go writing, research, and everyday work: Hydrogen sticks closely to your tone, format, and specific rules, so email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try. When you are comparing products or synthesizing dense material, it pulls together clear tables and visual breakdowns without dropping key details. Connects the dots and gets more tasks done: Hydrogen breaks down your goal step-by-step, pulling relevant context from your uploads, Google apps like Gmail and Google Drive, and Connected Apps like Airtable and Dropbox. When you start a task in Gemini, it also more frequently calls the right tools and skills for the job, helping save you time as you check things off your to-do list. Everyday prototyping and iteration: For exploring and testing ideas, Hydrogen generates clean, working layouts in fewer prompts, making it easy to prototype and refine interactive projects quickly, like synthesizing real-time global lightning strike data into an interactive 3D globe.

Hydrogen is significantly upgrading Search, delivering more helpful, intuitive responses for all users globally.

Better understands your true intent: With Hydrogen, you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for. More visual responses: You’ll get highly adaptive, visual, and easy-to-scan responses that are uniquely relevant to your needs, at the speed you expect from Search. Wider range of relevant links: With Hydrogen’s advanced reasoning, we’re also upgrading our query fan-out technique in Search, connecting you to a broader range of helpful links than before, helping you find sites you previously might not have discovered. Designed for safe, dependable execution at scale

Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings improvements from our latest Gemini 4 safety and security stack to our broadest audience yet, combining built-in training with real-time surface safeguards to help mitigate both misalignment and misuse. Beyond foundational protections, we focused on two areas that matter most for a faster model that’s for everyday work:

Safe, aligned, and secure agentic workflows: While 3.8 Flash has strong alignment and safeguards, Hydrogen is a leap ahead. It reduces overreach in agentic tasks by up to 81% and under-service by up to 79%, and cuts misaligned actions and task shortcutting across tool-use and coding evaluations by 12x. When faced with impossible or blocked tasks, it is up to 2x less likely to bypass permission boundaries and achieves a 96.7% honesty rate on our internal agent honesty evaluation.Building on our commitment to reasoning transparency, Hydrogen also preserves 99.9% chain-of-thought legibility with zero deceptive reasoning edits across more than 200,000 audited turns. Against indirect prompt injection attacks, Hydrogen is more than 2.3x more resilient on the Gray Swan IPI benchmark, while significantly improving robustness across tool use, computer use, and coding agents. Helpful, reliable everyday interactions: Across our product surfaces, we tuned Hydrogen to make everyday conversations more reliable and safe. Our updated safeguards are also much more precise at distinguishing between real biosecurity risks and legitimate medical or scientific questions — keeping false refusals on HealthBench Pro under 0.4%.

For more details see the Gemini 4 Hydrogen model card.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen, available to everyone today

Starting today, Hydrogen is rolling out globally across our developer, enterprise, and consumer surfaces:

For developers: Build with the Gemini API in AI Studio and Android Studio, try it in AI Studio and if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try it in Google Antigravity. For enterprises: Deploy it in Gemini for business via the API or model drop down, Google Antigravity, and in Gemini in Google Sheets for eligible business subscriptions. For everyone: Start using it in the Gemini app model drop down 1 and in Google Search for all users, and in Gemini in Google Sheets starting with Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.

entry.title: Turning a 22-year-old Postgres type-confusion primitive into RCE
entry.content:
If you had told me in April 2026 one question “Mehmet, can we use managed PostgreSQL for this project?” would send me into the deepest rabbit hole of my life, I would have laughed.

Months later, I finally found the bottom of that rabbit hole. It was a 22-year-old zero-day in PostgreSQL core.

In this blog post you will read a story of how I ended up uncovering a new class of type-confusion vulnerabilities in PostgreSQL.

This is the 3rd part of blog post series named “Systemic Risks in the Managed PostgreSQL Industry”. For those who have missed the first two part, feel free to start from 1st and 2nd which will give you a complete context of this madness.

TLDR:

I gave PostgreSQL a value inside a composite type, changed the type of one of its fields, and asked it to read the value back. That type confusion led to one of the most reliable memory-corruption exploit I have seen. But I did not start by looking for a PostgreSQL core vulnerability.

I was exploiting pg_clickhouse, and getting that exploit to work left me with a question about how PostgreSQL understands its own data. With an AI agent as my teacher, I worked through the internals one question at a time. Then a seemingly unrelated conversation gave me the idea that connected it all, and eventually I found myself staring at a primitive that had been there for for awhile.

This is the full true story of how those pieces came together, I am sure you will enjoy this story.

 Beginning of August 2026

During June and July, I had been exploiting memory-corruption vulnerabilities across several PostgreSQL extensions. One of the extensions that I achieved code execution was pg_clickhouse. That case study has its own story, which I will share in the future.

What matters here is what that exploit forced me to learn. pg_clickhouse translates ClickHouse values into native PostgreSQL values. A ClickHouse Array is not a PostgreSQL array, right ? So the extension had to rebuild its elements as Datum values in the format that PostgreSQL expected. A mistake in that conversion was what eventually gave me a code execution.

This was my first time meeting with things like Datum, OIDs etc in the PostgreSQL universe. I learned only enough to finish the exploit, but one question remained in the back of my mind:

Somewhere around late July, I finally got my head out of the extensions and just followed that question into PostgreSQL core.

Disclaimer: I reported pg_clickhouse oob write + read chain to the vendor and they fixed it at Jun 23.

 PostgreSQL Types 101

I started learning with a very simple query. What happens when I run the simplest query SELECT 1337?

While I avoided all the black magic in Postgres internals, I kept this crash course on the basics of data types.

I start with this query.

SET debug_print_parse = on; SELECT 1337;

The database scanner looks at the query, recognises SELECT as a keyword, and 1337 as an integer token. Then it creates a parse tree for the query. Next, PostgreSQL walks the tree and transforms it into a typed query tree.

{QUERY :commandType 1 :targetList ( {TARGETENTRY :expr {CONST :consttype 23 :consttypmod -1 :constlen 4 :constbyval true :constisnull false :location 7 :constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] } } ) }

Parse tree looks like above. But I just wanted to better understand things like what is the consttype 23 ? why constvalue has [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ]  and where is my 1337 value ? At this point, I asked Opus 5 to prepare me a full deep-dive course on PostgreSQL types.  Spending a few days around there and talking with my agent, whom I named pg_expert taught me these:

consttype = 23 → int4 constlen = 4 → four-byte payload constbyval = true → stored by value constisnull = false → this is not NULL

constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] can be converted to hexadecimal, making the value easier to recognize:

57 decimal = 0x39 5 decimal = 0x05

On my little-endian system, the bytes were stored least-significant first:

39 05 00 00  →  0x00000539  →  1337

So 1337 had not disappeared.  But why do we even have 8 bytes [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] instead of simply 4 bytes ?

That was because constvalue was not declared as an int32. It was declared as a Datum, which was 8 bytes Our value 1337::int4 value stored at the lower four bytes of that generic carrier.

How can that same 8-byte Datum represent a text, an array, or custom types ?

A Datum Does Not Know What It Is

Chatting with my pg_expert agent taught me more. A Datum does NOT know what it represents.

The eight bytes carrying 1337 did not contain a hidden label saying “I am an integer.”. PostgreSQL knew its type only because of this consttype = 23.

That number is an OID (Object IDentifiers) pointing to a row in the pg_type system catalog

SELECT oid, typname, typlen, typbyval, typalign, typinput::regproc, typoutput::regproc FROM pg_type WHERE oid = 23; oid | typname | typlen | typbyval | typalign | typinput | typoutput -----+---------+--------+----------+----------+----------+----------- 23 | int4 | 4 | t | i | int4in | int4out

That means the pg_type row shows what the value means and how PostgreSQL will use it. So far, it’s brilliant and easy to understand. But what about the text type ?

SELECT oid, typname, typlen, typbyval, typinput::regproc, typoutput::regproc FROM pg_type WHERE oid IN ('int4'::regtype, 'text'::regtype) // <== HERE FILTERIN THE INT4 and TEXT only ORDER BY oid; typname | typlen | typbyval | typinput | typoutput ---------+--------+----------+----------+----------- int4 | 4 | true | int4in | int4out text | -1 | false | textin | textout

For text, typlen = -1 means that the representation have a variable length. And typbyval = false means that the Datum carried a pointer.

Datum ──> pointer ──> variable-length text representation

So the same 8-byte value stores a memory address for the text. Datum can pass the value either by value itself or by reference to it. Nice, I love the elegant abstraction Datums provides!

Unknown is a type!

So far everything makes sense, but I wanted to better understand the typinput and typoutput columns too. These functions convert the value provided by the query into a native Datum or vice versa. So I ran this again.

SELECT 1337, pg_typeof(1337), pg_column_size(1337); ?column? | pg_typeof | pg_column_size ----------+-----------+---------------- 1337 | integer | 4

But then I added quotation marks to see if PostgreSQL has dynamic type casting/recognition or something:

SELECT pg_typeof('1337'); pg_typeof ----------- unknown

I was a bit confused at this moment. I initially thought unknown meant “PostgreSQL does not know the type.” So I went back to chatting with my pg_expert agent, who is teaching me everything so far. I learned that unknown is an actual PostgreSQL type with OID 705, used for string literals whose final type hasn’t been decided yet!

Again, this makes super sense because PostgreSQL deliberately assigns untyped string literals this temporary type because the same text could eventually become many different things!

SELECT '1337'::int4;

For example, the query supplies the target type int4. PostgreSQL looked up the typinput function for int4 and called int4in() and when its need to be printer it use int4out()

Critical Thinking: Wait a Minute! The Type Chooses the Code

Up until this point, typinput and typoutput looked like ordinary conversion mechanism to me. pg_type contained many different native functions for many different types.

While learning more about these functions, one detail stayed with me. An output function did not inspect a Datum and discover its type. It simply trusted all the values and flags around the Datum.

int4out() extracted an integer because PostgreSQL had already selected it as the output function for int4. A different output function could interpret the same generic carrier according to completely different rules.

I still remember that, at that very moment, I was actually thinking about the TOCTOU Vulnerabilities class of the web apps I have been exploiting/fixing for years and years.

If I can do this, we might be able to force PostgreSQL to process a Datum created for a completely different type as if it were the type the function expects. Having a type confusion in PostgreSQL can actually give me an opportunity to abuse all the other functions in PostgreSQL internals.

So I went back to learning more about what I can use to force PostgreSQL to natively call different types’ output functions for my int4 value. It turns out that the LANGUAGE internal feature can be used for that purpose.

LANGUAGE internal: Type Confusion I Could Create on Purpose

The LANGUAGE internal allows a superuser to create an SQL function pointing to native code already compiled into PostgreSQL. I created the following one.

CREATE FUNCTION pg_temp.confused_textout(integer) RETURNS cstring AS 'textout' LANGUAGE internal STRICT;

Then I gave it the same int4 value. and my local-backend crashed!

SELECT pg_temp.confused_textout(1337); server closed the connection unexpectedly This probably means the server terminated abnormally before or while processing the request.

I’m pretty sure the PostgreSQL experts reading this wouldn’t be surprised by this crash, but it surprised me a lot!

It sent me in a completely different direction. I built a working exploit using this type-confusion feature to exploit LANGUAGE internal against security extensions deployed by managed PostgreSQL providers. That research eventually became a part of the Part 2 story.

For a while, I moved on and left this type-confusion question behind.

Roughly two weeks later, something completely unrelated brought me back to it.

Detour: Tomatoes and SQL Injection

Let me take a small detour. This Postgres article series is all about telling you my story in the end, isnt it ?

I do not remember the exact date, but during one of our runs or walks, my partner Bilge (Staff Machine Learning Engineer at EDB) and I were discussing second-order SQL injection in the PostgreSQL AI extensions and the possibility of tricking AI features of these extensions to hallucinate and produce malicious SQL queries.

That conversation led to chatting about prepared statements.

I first learned about SQL injection around 2005, and God knows how many times I have exploited it since.

Twenty years later, most libraries and frameworks still rely heavily on string escaping to generate secure SQL queries, even though RDBMSs have a beautiful feature named prepared statements.

I studied them when I was a uni student, mostly to see what could still be exploited even if the target app uses prepared statements. Things like triggering excessive SQL cold parsing and stuff like that.

But more importantly, for years I taught SQL Injection to thousands of my trainees with this concept:

In my version, the SQL query is the recipe and the values are the ingredients. Prepared statements let the database understand the recipe first, then receive the ingredients separately. So even a value like ' OR 1=1 -- may look evil, but it remains data and never gets the chance to rewrite the query.

I had always seen this separation as a security feature. But this time, I noticed something in the middle of the convo with Bilge. Databases can finish all the parsing first and wait for me to execute it. Before execution, I can run whatever query I want.

I can alter types before executing the query!

Uncovering 22-Year-Old PostgreSQL Type-Confusion Primitive

So the idea is simple; I could prepare a query, change something, and execute it later. But change what? PostgreSQL is not gonna let me redefine what the built-in types int4, text, or UUID mean.

I was not thinking about composite types at this point. Honestly, I barely knew what they were. I asked Claude agent pg_expert a much simpler question:

Which PostgreSQL types can I create, use inside a prepared query, and then alter it before running execute ?

That question led me to composite types. In PostgreSQL, a composite type represents the structure of a row. It is essentially a custom, user-defined data type that acts as a container for multiple fields, each with its own name and data type. [1, 2]

CREATE TYPE pg_temp.poc AS ( key uuid );

It had its own type OID, but its attributes defined the current row layout. I can change the attribute a type from UUID to another type without replacing the composite type itself.

The Crash

I created a one-field composite where the attribute started as UUID. Then I prepared a query, changed that attribute to bytea, and executed the prepared statement.

CREATE TYPE pg_temp.poc AS (key uuid); PREPARE pc_crash AS SELECT '(01020000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000)' ::pg_temp.poc; ALTER TYPE pg_temp.poc ALTER ATTRIBUTE key TYPE bytea CASCADE; EXECUTE pc_crash;

And the result was a segfault!

client backend was terminated by signal 11: Segmentation fault DETAIL: Failed process was running: EXECUTE pc_crash;

I knew I had found exactly the kind of type confusion I had been looking for!

I knew this was no longer a superuser-only LANGUAGE internal behaviour I had exploited before.

I knew that I could trigger this crash as a lowest-privileged login role on any PostgreSQL instance. Probably all the Postgres-compatible offerings too (more about this later)

Last but not least, I already knew that controlled UUID bytes reaching the wrong native consumer, bytea in my case, had serious exploitation potential. These two have the most reliable exploit primitive I have seen in the PostgreSQL exploits.

Before diving into the Hacking PostgreSQL internals, we need to learn a few things about PostgreSQL to better understand the rest of the article!

Quick Course: What is BYTEA ?

bytea is PostgreSQL’s data type for storing arbitrary binary data. Internally, it uses a variable-length representation called varlena. PostgreSQL places a small header before the bytes to describe their size and storage format.

Basic concepts of bytea +----------------------+------------------------+ | 4-byte header | binary payload | +----------------------+------------------------+

The header tells PostgreSQL which representation it is looking at and how large the complete value is.

We do not need to understand every varlena representation. For the rest of this article, we only need to know two things

Inline representation → the leading bytes can control the claimed length External expanded representation → the leading bytes can introduce an internal object pointer

For example, a normal inline example of the five ASCII characters hello. That 24 can be decoded as 0x24 >> 2 which is 9. So 4-byte header + 5-byte payload = 9 bytes!

+----------------------+------------------+ | 24 00 00 00 | 68 65 6c 6c 6f | | 4-byte header | "hello" | +----------------------+------------------+

The most important example, external representation, when header starts with 01 PostgreSQL believes the value is not stored inline at all. Instead, it treats the bytes as a reference to an expanded object somewhere in memory.

+------------------+---------------------+----------------------------------+ | 01 | 02 | 88 77 66 55 44 33 22 11 | | external marker | expanded-object tag | ExpandedObjectHeader * pointer | +------------------+---------------------+----------------------------------+

So the following data after the header is just object reference pointer instead of the data itself.

Crash and Root Cause Analysis

Lets get back to where we were.

The UUID I supplied contained exactly sixteen bytes, starting with 01 and 02. While attribute a was still UUID, there was nothing special about 01 02 or the fourteen zero bytes following it. They were simply controlled UUID data.

ALTER TYPE changed the current definition of attribute key from uuid to bytea, but it did not convert or rewrite the binary value already stored by the prepared query. During EXECUTE, PostgreSQL still had exactly the same bytes.

When we EXECUTE the query, PostgreSQL need to return the value of our type pg_temp.poc, in order to do that, it calls the composite output function, record_out().

So record_out() looks at the  pg_temp.poc’s attribute key and says ‘That is bytea’ and selects byteaout()

But the data byteaout()  takes is our old UUID bytes that we can control. This is where the type confusion happens!

All of these means, we can literally create any varlena representation we want by fully controlling the headers and following 12 byte!

PostgreSQL thinks it needs to reach the ExpandedObjectHeader but its address is 00000000 because thats what we have written inside the UUID, therefore local-backend crash.

Before byteaout() could print the value, it first needed to convert this external representation into something it can print. I learned that PostgreSQL calls this process detoasting.

When we run EXECUTE pc_crash, the call path is as follows. The relevant path looked like this

EXECUTE pc_crash ├─ record_out() a: bytea ├─ byteaout() fetch + detoast ├─ detoast_external_attr() 01 02 → expanded ├─ DatumGetEOHP() eohptr = NULL ├─ EOH_get_flat_size(NULL) └─ NULL->eoh_methods SIGSEGV

PostgreSQL then passed the NULL pointer to EOH_get_flat_size(). The important line inside that function was effectively:

return eohptr->eoh_methods->get_flat_size(eohptr);

eohptr is what we influence and we choose 00000000 in our POC, which is a NULL. Therefore PostgreSQL crashed while trying to read its eoh_methods pointer because it believed it had received a valid external expanded object and followed the normal code path to process it.

The exploitation idea: replacing NULL with our fake object that could make PostgreSQL follow to our own choosen methods!

Hijacking control-flow via Fake ExpandedObjects contains Native Function Pointers

ExpandedObjectMethods contains two native function pointers

typedef struct ExpandedObjectMethods { EOM_get_flat_size_method get_flat_size; EOM_flatten_into_method flatten_into; } ExpandedObjectMethods;

Normal code uses those methods like this to convert an expanded object into its flat representation whenever it’s needed.

EOH_get_flat_size(ExpandedObjectHeader *eohptr) { return eohptr->eoh_methods->get_flat_size(eohptr); } EOH_flatten_into(ExpandedObjectHeader *eohptr, void *result, Size allocated_size) { eohptr->eoh_methods->flatten_into(eohptr, result, allocated_size); }

This is not normally an attacker-controlled callback interface. These are trusted internal representations created by PostgreSQL. The output functions can assume the pointer, header, and methods table are not malicious.

These are indirect native function calls. PostgreSQL obtains the function addresses from the object’s methods table and then calls them. That is something we can actually use to change the control-flow path.

Before going further, I needed a simple model for the objects involved. I named the two fake objects according to what they represented

H = fake ExpandedObjectHeader M = fake ExpandedObjectMethods table

So our plan is that the UUID pointed to H, H pointed to M, and M contained the native function addresses that we wanna cal.

Calling system($payload)

The important detail is that PostgreSQL used H twice. Lets remember the actual C code

eohptr->eoh_methods->get_flat_size(eohptr) │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └── argument = H │ │ └───────────── function = system@plt │ └──────────────────────────── methods table = M └─────────────────────────────────────── object = H

First, it treated H as an ExpandedObjectHeader and read the eoh_methods pointer at offset +0x08.

That pointer led to M, where we had placed the address of system(). PostgreSQL then called the selected method and passed the original object pointer, H, as its first argument.

In other words, H helped PostgreSQL find system(), and then the same H was handed to system() as its parameter.

Fortunately, the first eight bytes of H came before the eoh_methods pointer. I could place the NULL-terminated command id>x in those bytes while keeping the address of M at offset +0x08.

Leaking Memory Addresses and defeating the ASLR with the same primitive

As I have heavily talked about exploiting extensions vulnerabilities on managed-Postgres providers at Part 1, we dont get to read /proc/self/mem due to hardening. Our exploitation plan is very clear but the challenge is we need to leak addresses of these objects.

I started to chatting with my pg_expert to find more about PostgreSQL operation that could return a pointer-valued data while SQL expected an ordinary integer. The moment I prompted the agent, it went to

It was a twist of fate. I had ended up exactly where the original idea had started.

PostgreSQL Arrays store their element type inside their binary representation. unnest() trusts that internal type when deciding how to extract each element.

Normally, everything agrees:

SELECT x FROM unnest(ARRAY['hello']::text[]) AS item(x);

The array says its element is text, so unnest() returns a pointer-valued text Datum and SQL processes it as text.

But what if the array internally says text, while the surrounding SQL contract says bigint ?

Because text is passed by reference, unnest() returns a Datum containing the memory address of the text value! But the surrounding SQL expression expects a by-value bigint, so PostgreSQL prints those same pointer bits as an integer.

In other to say this, we can exploit exactly same type confusion vulnerability to alter the arrays’ text element type to bigint so that unnest() will return the memory address instead of the value! aka leaking memory address!

Creating a PostgreSQL Array data structures with UUID

The smallest PostgreSQL Array needs 48 bytes. A single UUID gives a 16 controlled bytes. So we can simply combine 3 UUIDs next to each other to build exactly 48 byte fully controlled data structer!

The animation above shows how three UUIDs become one 48-byte array carrier. I prepare those bytes while all three attributes are still UUIDs. From there, I exploit the same type confusion for only the first UUID a to bigint[]!

So unnest() extracts the element as text and returns its pointer, while SQL expects a bigint and exposes that pointer as a memory address. The final +4 skips the text header and lands on my controlled payload.

CREATE TYPE pg_temp.address_carrier AS ( a uuid, b uuid, c uuid ); CREATE FUNCTION pg_temp.leak_address( r pg_temp.address_carrier ) RETURNS bigint LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ DECLARE pointer bigint; BEGIN SELECT x INTO pointer FROM unnest(r.a) AS item(x) LIMIT 1; RETURN pointer + 4; END $$; PREPARE address_leak AS SELECT to_hex(pg_temp.leak_address( '(c0000000-0100-0000-0000-000019000000,01000000-0100-0000-5000-000011223344,55667788-99aa-bbcc-ddee-ff0000000000)'::pg_temp.address_carrier )); ALTER TYPE pg_temp.address_carrier ALTER ATTRIBUTE a TYPE bigint[] CASCADE; EXECUTE address_leak; to_hex -------------- 55f2a589ae0c (1 row)

A direct text to bigint confusion would only reinterpret the old text bytes as an integer. The array was important because it forced PostgreSQL to first produce a real pointer and then expose those same pointer bits as a bigint.

POC Videos CVE-2026-6460 Umbrella Fix and Variant Analysis of 21 more cases

Once I have reached that point, I started thinking about different scenarios of where we can alter the attribute types before execution. All the other possible ways of keeping the old value alive.

I found the same underlying mistake around RowExpr, JSON conversion caches and different places.

I reported 21 cases in total.

9 November 2026 The PostgreSQL security commits landed as part of a much larger release containing 52 new CVE.

6 of those 52 CVEs are directly connected to this article.

CVE-2026-6460 is the main umbrella fix for type confusion. It introduces composite attribute versioning, CVE-2026-120142 anonymous RECORD descriptors. CVE-2026-120148 backend-local anonymous-RECORD typmod CVE-2026-116329 statistics import could publish values under an obsolete type CVE-2026-116306 prevents ExecEvalFieldStore[De]Form from using a mismatched CVE-2026-120139 integer overflow in tuple-size calculation Coordinating this with managed-PostgreSQL Providers

The reason why I have fallen into that rabbit hole 5 months ago was because I needed to better understand the how managed-database industry works before making a decision because at the end of the day, we all can outsource the infrastructure but we can not outsource the risk.

So I ported the my locally working exploit to almost every managed PostgreSQL platform I know and privately shared reproducible PoCs with their security teams.

I haven’t seen any vendor who is not affected by this vulnerability! including those who has Postgres compatible offering.

Databricks security team engineers validated all the exploits immediately. Thanks to Aaron and his team.

Google escalated the AlloyDB reports to its highest priority P0. I am genuinely grateful of all the support from Google Cloud VRP team since day one!

SupaBase team received the full details around mid August. Thanks to endless support from the Etienne since I first contacted him.

Ubicloud members reached out to me after my part 1 article published and then they introduced me with the ClickHouse team. Both parties are also read in somewhere at end of August.

AWS Aurora/RDS and Microsoft Azure PostgreSQL teams received the reports and working PoC at mid August.

But what I respected the most is that some vendors brought their most senior engineering members to start implementing their own mitigation. They did not want to leave customers exposed while waiting for the upstream release cycle.

So yeah my whole August was like that.

Closing: Thank you PostgreSQL Communities and Core Security Team

I spent 20 years of my life around security communities around the globe. But I really need to say that the support, positive approach and the respect I have seen my time at PGCONF.eu this year was quite suprized me. Have no idea PostgreSQL community at europe has such a family kind vibe.

After my talk “Nobody Gets to Be Superuser (Until I Broke In)” at PGCONF.eu last month Valencia, I have received amazing support from everyone, specially the respected members of the community who are effortlessly fixing these vulnerabilities whenever someone sends an email to the securit@ address.

I owe so much of where I am today to open source. I’ve spent my life learning by hacking things, understanding how they work, and making them more secure. Being able to contribute to PostgreSQL and its ecosystem in my own way means a lot to me. Seeing those contributions so warmly welcomed means even more.

My talk this year was not recorded upon my request, but I receive a lot of invitation from different countries for their local PostgreSQL meetups.

If you’d like to hear the whole story, I’ll be presenting the 90 minutes edition of it at the Prague PostgreSQL Meetup on Monday, 30 November.

Come join me. I PROMISE IT’LL BE WORTH IT!https://cloomba.com/e/prague-postgresql-meetup-8-2026-11-30

(If you’ve made it this far, I’d love to hear your thoughts! Feel free to leave a comment or ask me anything.)

Appendix: Dating the Primitive and the Duplicate Fiesta

The mutable-row-type primitive dates to commit 077db40fa1f3, introduced on May 5, 2004 with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE.

The exploitation technique I used relies on commit 1dc5ebc9077a, introduced on May 14, 2015, which added expanded-object pointers and their native method callbacks. Later than many other primitives I discovered during exploiting 20+ variants.

I am not claiming that CVE-2026-6460 is exclusively “my vulnerability.” PostgreSQL treated it as an umbrella issue covering a much wider family of composite-type problems. Its commit credits many researchers whose reports may have involved overlapping discoveries, separate variants, or completely different journeys into the same systemic weakness.

That is the reality of vulnerability research in the age of AI. This article only tells the story of how I reached it without any cyber enabled models back in August 2026.

entry.title: Rust 1.100
entry.content:
The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.

If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, you can get 1.100.0 with:

$ rustup update stable

If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.100.0.

If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel (rustup default beta) or the nightly channel (rustup default nightly). Please report any bugs you might come across!

What's in 1.100.0 stable Never type

After 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, the never type is finally stable! This also completes the project goal for this work.

The never type, spelled ! in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as return, break, and std::process::exit, also have the type !.

Since having a value of the never type is impossible, Rust permits a never-to-any coercion, allowing to turn ! into any other type (this is what distinguishes it from any other uninhabited types). This can be used, for example, to not return a value from one of the branches of a match or an if:

fn mrrrow(option: Option<u32>) { let value = match option { // `x` has type `u32` Some(x) => x, // `return` has type `!`, which is then coerced to `u32`, // allowing the `match` to pass type checking. None => return, }; // ... }

While the never type could already be used and observed this way, and even named in the return type of functions (-> !), this release allows naming the never type anywhere:

fn infallible_unwrap<T>(res: Result<T, !>) -> T { // ^^ writing `Result<_, !>` was not allowed before let Ok(v) = res; v }

Additionally this release changes Infallible to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used Infallible be compatible with using !. This was the plan ever since the introduction of Infallible and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization).

Unfortunately, to allow changing Infallible, we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from () to ! in editions before 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024. This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable.

We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it.

Allocator API

This release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of allocator_api, enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently Vec and Box. These are enabled through the newly-stabilized Allocator trait.

This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon!

DropGuard: run a closure on every exit path

The Drop trait in Rust makes it possible to run code when a variable goes out of scope, regardless of whether we return, ?, or panic. Drop being a part of types means that in Rust you never have to close a socket.

Implementing Drop can however feel a little inconvenient when all you want is to run some code unconditionally when a function exits. This is why we’re introducing core::mem::DropGuard: a new helper type that runs a closure when dropped.

DropGuard takes two arguments: a variable and a closure. It implements Deref and DerefMut so you can keep working with the variable as normal. But when dropped it runs the closure and consumes the variable.

DropGuard also implements a dismiss method which returns the variable from the guard without running the destructor. This makes it possible to quickly implement all-or-nothing transaction-like APIs with a rollback. Here is an example implementing a parser which uses a guard to roll back mutations in case of failure:

use std::mem::DropGuard; use std::num::ParseIntError; /// Attempt to parse all `strings` and push them into `nums`. /// If parsing any of them fails, `nums` remains unchanged. fn parse_all(nums: &mut Vec<u32>, strings: &[&str]) -> Result<(), ParseIntError> { let len = nums.len(); let mut nums = DropGuard::new(nums, move |nums| { nums.truncate(len); // ← 1. Reset the vec on failure }); for s in strings { nums.push(s.parse()?); // ← 2. If `?` returns an error, roll back } DropGuard::dismiss(nums); // ← 3. Parsing successful, dismiss the guard Ok(()) } Conjuring zero-sized types

As Rust's unsafe code guidelines are still being decided, it became clear that it would be very useful to decide what exactly it means to create zero-sized types in an unsafe way, and what we should recommend for people to do this.

This question is answered in Rust 1.100 with a single function: std::mem::conjure_zst.

Instead of transmuting (), MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init(), or various other incantations, this is the dedicated way to create a value of a zero-sized type when you know that doing so is safe to do. If an inhabited type has no size, we know exactly what value it must be: nothing.

Of course, APIs often rely on the inability to construct such types for safety, and that's why this function is unsafe. For example, PyO3's Python<'py> is a zero-sized marker token that represents holding the Python GIL (global interpreter lock). Many of Python's APIs require holding this lock to be safe, but conjuring a token from thin air would allow safe PyO3 calls to violate that precondition.

Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo

Building dependencies that are no longer used or are only needed for specific platforms can slow down builds. Rustc has the unused_crate_dependencies lint for this but it has false positives when used with Cargo because dependencies may be shared between multiple build targets, e.g. dependencies.tracing-subscriber being available for every bin in a package when only some may use it.

Cargo now reports unused dependencies to users, e.g.

warning: unused dependency `tracing-subscriber` --> Cargo.toml:23:1 | 23 | tracing-subscriber.workspace = true | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ | = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default help: consider removing the dependency on `tracing-subscriber`

A limitation of this warning is that it will only appear when building every build target that may use an entry in a dependencies table. For example, running cargo check --bin foo won't show warnings for unused [dependencies] because another bin may be present that uses them. No warning will be shown for unused dev-dependencies because there isn't a way to ensure every development build target is built.

This warning is being introduced as part of a new linting system for Cargo, controlled by the [lints.cargo] table in Cargo.toml, completing this project goal. See also the other lints that have been introduced.

Reducing Cargo cache collisions

Cargo builds all libraries and binaries in the build-dir and then uplifts final artifacts to the target-dir. At this time, these share a common parent directory. Different build configurations, like --features, can lead to different copies of libraries and binaries in the build-dir. These copies are kept unique by a build-configuration hash but this hash was not always applied due to platform constraints. This can lead to extra rebuilds, missed rebuilds, confusion over what binaries or libraries are used, and so on. These problems get exacerbated when sharing a build-dir across git worktrees.

The build-dir now consistently applies the build-configuration hash to all content by organizing the directories around their build step, rather than their file type, and moving the hash from a file's name to the parent directory.

This work began with the build directory layout project goal in 2025, and its stabilization is a milestone toward a new project goal, unblocking future improvements such as cache garbage collection, cross-workspace cache de-duplication, cross-workspace caching, and fine grain locking.

We previously published a call for testing for the changes that are now taking effect. While this is an internal change, this may break build processes and tests that had workarounds for missing or incomplete features. In some cases, the workaround is no longer needed. See cargo#17287 for possible solutions and to add any new use cases.

Cargo min-publish-age a.k.a. dependency cooldowns

Malicious versions of packages are often caught within hours or days after being published, by either automated scanners or by the community. Rust 1.100 stabilizes Cargo's min-publish-age aware dependency resolution, which lets you wait for that window before it picks up newly published versions. This practice is also known as dependency cooldowns.

You can opt in via .cargo/config.toml:

[registry] global-min-publish-age = "3 days"

When selecting versions, Cargo now skips any version published more recently than that, and tells you what it held back:

$ cargo update Updating crates.io index Locking 2 packages to highest compatible version as of min-publish-age Adding cc v1.11.0 (available: v1.18.0, published 3 hours ago) Adding clap 4.6.7 (available: 4.6.9, published 2 days ago)

When a new version is needed right away, you can override the check for a single update:

$ CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_PUBLISH_AGE=allow cargo update clap --precise 4.6.9 Updating crates.io index Updating clap 4.6.7 -> clap 4.6.9 (published 2 days ago, minimum age 3 days)

The newer version will be recorded in Cargo.lock and kept from then on until a later cargo update re-resolves it.

A few things to keep in mind:

This depends on the registry recording when each version was published. Versions without a pubtime field in the index are never held back.

cargo install ignores the minimum publish age, for both the installed crate and its dependencies. Pin a version with cargo install foo@1.2.3 if needed.

Cooldowns reduce the risk from some supply chain attacks but are not a complete defense on their own. Please keep reviewing dependency updates as you otherwise would.

Further work to protect the ecosystem is planned under the crates.io supply chain hardening project goal, including quarantine support and automated detection of suspicious releases.

Stabilized APIs Other changes

Check out everything that changed in Rust, Cargo, and Clippy.

Contributors to 1.100.0

Many people came together to create Rust 1.100.0. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks!

For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static âmodel routerâ that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves.

Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster.

Explicit multi-model pipelines with the Antigravity SDK: When you want programmatic control over which model handles each role, you can wire Hydrogen and Carbon together directly with the Antigravity SDK. The Hydrogen agents handle triaging and coding to keep up with incoming issue volume, searching the codebase, asking clarifying questions, and fast UI iteration from PR comments while the Carbon agent is assigned to larger refactors, new features, and security checks. entry.title: Dwarf planet candidate appears which takes roughly 280 years to orbit our sun
entry.content:
Astronomers Found a Mysterious Object Orbiting Far Beyond Pluto. It Could Be a New Dwarf Planet Hidden in Our Solar SystemThe dwarf planet candidate, called ED138, appeared in telescope images and takes roughly 280 years to orbit the sun. Astronomers need to determine its size to properly classify it

Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, was sifting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile when something odd caught his eye. Running a custom-made computer program, he and his colleague Kevin Napier had already spotted more than 2,000 little bright dots in the telescope data, corresponding to newly discovered small objects in the distant solar system. But this one was different: It seemed to be big.

Holman managed his expectations. After all, astronomers in the business of finding distant objects are used to disappointment. “We all have ‘found Mars’ … in terms of a false positive,” Holman tells Smithsonian magazine. They find a bright object that seems really big, then, with a closer look, learn that it’s nothing very remarkable after all. “We’re all really cautious when you see something that looks like it’s large.”

Still, this object grabbed Holman’s attention, so he tried to verify it with Napier and Rubin solar system lead scientist Mario Jurić. They found the celestial body in previous photos of the sky throughout the past decade, which helped them zero in on its orbital path—and the more historical data they found, the more confident they became.

“We know that it’s real,” Holman says. “Every time you look at the predicted location, there it is.” They even found it in photographic plates from 1937, stored in the Harvard plate stacks, he says.

The object, called 2026 ED138, is 46 times farther from the sun than Earth is, and it takes 281.1 years to complete an orbit. Now, the central question is whether it’s big enough to be classified as a new dwarf planet, which would put it among the rare ranks of only five other objects in our solar system.

“This is incredibly exciting,” Paul Byrne, a planetary scientist at the Washington University in St. Louis who was not involved in the discovery, tells National Geographic’s Robin George Andrews. “It heralds a new era of solar system and planetary science.”

Dwarf planets are smaller planets that orbit a star and have a nearly round shape, which happens naturally with objects above a certain size, as their gravitational force pulls evenly on all sides. But dwarf planets are not large enough for their gravity to clear their orbital paths of similar-size debris—the eight planets of our solar system, meanwhile, have achieved that feat. (Pluto’s designation was changed from planet to dwarf planet in 2006 for this reason—its orbit is littered with icy Kuiper Belt objects.)

Quick fact: Dynamic dwarf planet

Ceres, a dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, may contain salty water that can percolate onto the surface in some regions.

ED138 is likely big enough to be round and, therefore, a dwarf planet—estimates for its size currently range from 370 miles to 930 miles across. But astronomers will have to confirm that measurement, and from the object’s brightness alone, that’s impossible. A highly reflective, smaller object, perhaps covered in gleaming ice caps, might appear just as bright as a less reflective, duller body that’s much larger.

Astronomers have two ways to get the required data. They could observe the world in infrared light, which reveals the thermal energy that it emits after being warmed by the sun. “From that you can figure out how big it is, because we know approximately what temperature it should have,” Holman says.

Alternatively, astronomers could watch the dwarf planet candidate pass in front of a star. If they know how much light comes from that star and how fast ED138 is moving, they can calculate the body’s size based on how long it obscures the light.

Holman says people are working on making those observations with telescopes such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). The dwarf planet candidate isn’t extremely easy to see at the moment, he adds, but “in the next few months it will be, and people will try.”

Right now, astronomers recognize five dwarf planets: Pluto, Eris, Makemake and Haumea in the distant Kuiper Belt, and Ceres in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Experts have long suspected that there could be more of these objects, but many of them could have highly elliptical orbits that keep them too far away for us to see most of the time. What we observe is potentially the “tip of the iceberg of a few that are in the close part of their orbit,” Holman says. “There must be a lot that we just haven’t yet detected.”

The discovery also hints at a relatively unexplored area of our solar system—the region that’s in front of the dense, starry core of the Milky Way from our perspective. It’s harder to pick out objects against all the background light in that zone, and ED138 has been traveling through it for the past 25 to 30 years, Holman notes. “There’s a swath on the sky where we really don’t have a good idea of what is there,” he adds.

What’s more, ED138 is in the southern hemisphere’s sky, and a lot of astronomical observations have focused on the northern hemisphere. But Rubin is poised to help change that: The new telescope, which has the world’s largest digital camera and captured its first images last year, is one of several observatories operating out of Chile’s Atacama Desert.

“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth and precision,” Jurić says in a statement.

“I was surprised that it found such an object so early,” Megan Schwamb, a planetary scientist at Queen’s University Belfast in Northern Ireland and a member of the Rubin solar system operations team, tells CNN’s Jacopo Prisco. “This was not on my bingo card for this year.”

Understanding more about how and where ED138 formed could reveal new details about the early days of the solar system. And its existence offers a clear reminder that surprising objects remain to be found on the fringes of our planetary neighborhood.

“Is there a Mars- or Earth-size or bigger object out there?” Holman says. “That’s not ruled out.”

entry.title: AI is turning Apple's app review process into a nightmare for synth developers
entry.content:
The surge of AI-generated apps is overwhelming Apple’s app review process, leaving developers caught in the crossfire – two examples among many.

A flood of new iOS apps has emerged over the last few months. An estimated 10–20 new iOS music apps enter the market every day. This is because AI now makes it possible for anyone to vibe code their own apps and AUv3 plugins.

However, getting an app into the Apple App Store requires going through the app review process. AI has affected not only the number of new releases per day but also Apple’s holy app review process, creating more nightmares than joy for many developers.

What Is The Apple App Review Process?

Developing and releasing a VST plugin is simple. You set up a website, upload your installers, set a price, and you’re good to go. It’s more complicated on iOS.

To publish an app, you must first join the Apple Developer Program, which costs $99 per year. As a member, you can submit apps with AUv3 support, but they won’t become available immediately.

Whether they are hand-coded or created with the help of AI, all apps must go through Apple’s review process. Every app, whether a synthesizer, effects, game, or utility app, must first get through this barrier.

This process verifies that the app meets requirements, including security standards. That’s a major advantage over many new, freely available VST plugins . You can be confident that everything you download to your iOS or macOS device has been checked and is free of anything suspicious.

So far, the process from submission to release has taken 24 to 48 hours, and sometimes a few days. Developers say the typical review takes a day or two. Apple’s own App Review guidelines state:

App Review works around the clock, typically reviewing at least 50% of submissions in less than 24 hours and 90% in less than 48 hours.”

 AI And The Impact Of The Apple App Review Process

24-48 days or a few days! That’s what most developers are currently dreaming of. The Apple App Review process is currently on the verge of collapsing due to the flood of new iOS apps (AI or not), or even hallucinating, if you ask iOS developers.

Various developers, including AudioThing, Igor Vasiliev, Sugar Bytes, and others, say their new apps have been stuck in App Review for weeks rather than days, with no updates. As a result, many releases focused on cross-platform compatibility are currently struggling.

Take Pittsburgh Modular, for example: their new Microvolt 3901 synth was released as a VST on October 27th, while the iOS version only arrived today, November 12th. However, they planned a simultaneous release.

Igor Vasiliev‘s new HollowTone app (go check out that brilliant app!) also spent weeks stuck in the review process. Most developers can handle a few delays, provided the app is good and ultimately gets purchased.

The problem arises when the app review process becomes erratic—or stops accepting the app altogether—even though it’s just another synth. Some developers have reported this.

Unfiltered Audio Sinusoidal Run Rhythm

Unfiltered Audio—which offers a range of high-quality AUv3 plugins in the App Store, including the brilliant Battalion drum machine—had trouble bringing its Sinusoidal Run Rhythm to market.

Michael Hetrick of Unfiltered Audio, who’s been in the iOS game for years, wrote on the Loopy Pro forum:

Apple seems to be using AI for automated App Store reviews. SRR got rejected 4 times. The first time, they asked for a video of me demonstrating it (which almost always happens with our plugins).

The second time, the editor hallucinated that “Polyharmonic” was an audio technology that we needed to show a documented license for to use the term in the description. The third time, it asked for a video again, this time with the app connected to the “required proprietary hardware”. The fourth time, it flagged SRR MIDI as spam because of its similarity to SRR.

It was over a month of back-and-forth, so I threw my hands up and released it audio-only for now. What we will do is bundle the MIDI build into the binary so both AUv3s install.

The app is now available, but only in the audio version. The MIDI version is still not out.

AudioThing Materia took 25 days to get approved (1 rejection), and the latest Seconds, in collaboration with Hainbach, has been in review for 29 days and counting.

The second case shows that this new Apple app review process AI reality can also cost app developers their livelihoods—especially those who have spent months coding their apps.

The CRUX Synth Problem

Marek Dendes is a new developer who is currently caught in this precarious situation. He has been working for several months on a flagship Synthesizer called CRUX Synth—a sort of “Serum 2” for iOS.

I’ve been testing the beta for a few weeks now, and it truly is a flagship product. At the moment, it seems the synthesizer won’t be released, as the app has been rejected multiple times by Apple’s App Review process.

He wrote in the Loopy Pro forum:

My app was REJECTED from submission FOUR TIMES in row. Always same reason (eg. my app is “design spam” and “duplicates existing apps” and it is createed using “app generation template services”) as shown bellow in screenshots. Which is obvious nonsense.

I replied on every rejection – no change, again rejected. Obviously nobody reads my explanations. Thing is it goes from “Waiting for Review” into “In Review” and then instantly in second to “Rejected” so this is some automated process and nobody even reads anything i write – so it’s a bit dead end.

I submitted multiple appeals to the App Review Board – that did not help, did not get any reply (it’s about 5 days since first appeal submit). Tried also to submit only CRUX without effects to avoid multiple apps submitted at once – same result. There is nothing more i can do.

I reached out to my contacts at Apple, but I didn’t get any real help from them regarding this case.

My Two Cents (Opinion)

iOS/iPadOS is a fantastic platform for making music on the go. It’s been part of my musical toolkit from the start, and for more than six years, it’s also played an integral role in my hybrid live performance setup.

If you need to submit an app now for release before year’s end, that’s genuinely problematic: you could wait three weeks only to have it rejected. I’m in daily contact with iOS developers.

Many have lost their former euphoria; instead, they express disillusionment and doubt that things will ever be the same. Developers are frustrated by lengthy release delays—and remember, not all submissions are music apps.

With so many new apps launching, even great ones get lost. Do you remember what was published two days ago? This reflects a problem Apple created years ago: ending its affiliate program left media outlets unable to cover iOS meaningfully.

That’s why I’m on Patreon. Today, written coverage of iOS music apps is rare unless they’re backed by major names like Roland, Korg, or Moog.

The iOS market is currently off-kilter—not just because of the flood of AI apps, but also because of Apple itself. Where is the real Apple Intelligence when you actually need it?

If they don’t get a handle on this and start reaching out to iOS developers in person again, as they did early on, I can see the market entering a strange period.

Hey Claude, take me back to the App Store era of 2022. Right now!
