entry.title: Foundation Models framework
entry.content:
Get started with the Foundation Models framework

The Foundation Models framework is the best way to use any large language model in your app. Whether you’re generating a quick summary or creating dynamic agents, the framework has what you need.

The Foundation Models framework is a native Swift API for integrating any large language model into your app — including direct access to the Apple Foundation Models on-device and in Private Cloud Compute. Powerful capabilities like guided generation, tool calling, image understanding, and Dynamic Profiles are built in, so you have what you need to build unique experiences.

Multimodal prompts let you pass images alongside text so your app can reason about visual content. This opens up new categories of experiences you can build with image understanding — it's as simple as attaching an image to your prompt. The Vision framework is also integrated directly, giving your model purpose-built tools like OCR for precise text extraction and barcode readers for quick code scanning — all on-device.

The Foundation Models framework gives you direct access to the on-device foundation model at the core of Apple Intelligence so you can build experiences that are smart, private, and work without internet connectivity.

On-device models are highly useful for many tasks, yet sometimes you need a larger model for a more complex workflow. The Foundation Models framework now extends to server models — like Claude, Gemini, and more — all through the same Swift API, with full support for features like tool calling and guided generation. Any model provider can create a Swift package conforming to the Language Model protocol, a fundamental component of the framework that allows you to pick the right language model for your app.

For those just getting started, developers who are enrolled in the App Store Small Business Program and have fewer than two million first-time App Store downloads can access the Apple Foundation Models running on Private Cloud Compute with no cloud API cost.* This delivers frontier-level intelligence with unparalleled privacy protections, ensuring that your users' data is not stored or accessible to Apple or anyone else.

Learn more about Private Cloud Compute

Dynamic Profiles are new declarative APIs for continuously updating your session's model, tools, and instructions on the fly. Rather than creating a session with a fixed configuration, you define profiles — each with its own model, temperature, reasoning level, and toolset — and swap between them within a single continuous session. The session transcript is shared across every profile switch, so your app gets more contextual intelligence with less prompting. Dynamic Profiles are designed to be adaptable building blocks: use them to build AI agents, skills, or any other high-level abstraction your app needs.

The Evaluations framework gives you the ability to test your prompts and validate that your intelligence-powered features work correctly across dynamic conditions, going beyond what unit tests alone can catch. Whether you're iterating on instructions, switching models, or tuning a Dynamic Profile, Evaluations gives you confidence that your app's behavior holds up before you ship.

The new fm command line tool in macOS 27 lets you streamline scripting, automate model workflows, and accelerate your development without writing a line of app code. You can prototype quickly, giving you a fast path from idea to implementation.

To help you get started with adopting emerging AI patterns, the Foundation Models framework utilities package adds experimental abstractions on top of the framework — including custom skills, context management helpers, and a Chat Completions client that connects to a hosted model of your choice.

The Foundation Models SDK for Python extends the framework into the Python ecosystem, letting you integrate with popular tooling and evaluation packages in Python.

The Acceptable Use Requirements for the Foundation Models framework outline prohibited uses of Apple Foundation Models. Additionally, pursuant to Article 53(1)(b) of the AI Act, we make available information and documentation to providers of AI systems who intend to integrate AFM 3 Cloud into their AI systems.

entry.title: Show HN: RealtimeVAD – trading false positives for 110ms earlier end-of-speech
entry.content:
Know that the speaker stopped, about 100 ms before Silero does.

RealtimeSTT · RealtimeTTS · Live demo · Spec · LiveKit plugin

A voice assistant can't do anything until it knows the user has stopped talking. Speech recognition, the LLM call and the voice output all wait for that one decision, and a normal voice activity detector takes a few hundred milliseconds to make it.

RealtimeVAD makes it sooner. It keeps Silero VAD to decide what is speech, and adds a second, faster check: every 10 ms it compares the audio level with the room's noise and with the speaker's own level. The moment the audio goes quiet, you get an event, long before Silero's probability has fallen.

Input: 16 kHz mono audio in chunks of any size (float32, int16 or int16 bytes). Output: start, pause and end events, plus the audio of the running segment at any time. Lead: speech-off a median 100 ms before Silero's probability drops, and 206 ms before Silero's VADIterator reports the end, on 3,279 real turns. The end itself comes before Silero's in 82 % of turns, by a median 70 ms. Price: it also fires in short gaps between words, about ten times as often as Silero. Quiet input: a quiet speaker's soft word endings are not silence; on a noisy quiet line the lead is gone instead (details). Runs on: one CPU thread, far faster than realtime. Needs only numpy and onnxruntime; the Silero model is bundled, no torch. Status: alpha (0.0.5). The API may still change. demo.mp4

The video uses a synthetic voice and shows a median lead of 92 ms. The 100 ms above is the median on real voice-assistant turns.

demo/ runs this page on your own microphone. It shows, turn by turn, how much sooner RealtimeVAD knew that you stopped than Silero alone, on the same audio.

pip install realtimevad from RealtimeVAD import VAD vad = VAD() for chunk in microphone_chunks(): for event in vad.feed(chunk): if event.kind == "start": stream_to_asr(vad.audio()) # includes the audio just before speech began elif event.kind == "pause": speculate(vad.audio()) # the speaker may be done; this isn't the end yet elif event.kind == "end": finalize(event.segment.audio) Event Meaning When start Speech has begun After about 64 ms of confident speech, so clicks don't trigger it. Speech Silero is never confident about (a short "mm-hmm", a quiet phone voice) starts after about 0.13 s at half confidence, if it is clearly louder than the room pause The speaker may have stopped (speech-off) Within about 10 ms of the audio going quiet end The segment is over 0.24 s after speech-off, unless speech resumes. Never later than Silero alone onset Speech may have begun At the first confident frame, before start confirms it. Off by default: VAD(onset_events=True)

vad.audio() returns the running segment at any time, starting about 0.3 s before the speech. end carries the finished segment with its audio, start time, end time and the time the speech stopped.

If your assistant talks while the microphone is open, pass vad.feed(chunk, playback=True) for those chunks so its own voice is handled as possible echo. Every threshold and duration can be configured; SPEC.md lists what is guaranteed.

pause is early and often wrong, on purpose. It fires on every breath, every short gap between words and every stop consonant, so most pause events are followed by more speech.

Use it to start work you can cancel: finalize the transcript, call the LLM, prepare the voice output. Cancel when speech continues. A wrong pause then costs almost nothing, and a right one saves hundreds of milliseconds. Never treat it as the end of the turn. Only end closes a segment. Can't cancel quickly? Ignore pause and wait for end. The extra false alarms would cost you more than they save.

Change the import:

from silero_vad import load_silero_vad from RealtimeVAD import VADIterator # was: from silero_vad import VADIterator vad_iterator = VADIterator(load_silero_vad(), sampling_rate=16000) speech_dict = vad_iterator(chunk, return_seconds=True) # {'start': ...} / {'end': ...} / None

The constructor and the results stay the same, but end arrives as soon as the audio goes quiet. Without a model argument, it uses the bundled Silero model and doesn't need torch.

livekit-plugins-realtimevad/ is a VAD plugin: realtimevad.VAD.load() in place of silero.VAD.load(). Its README shows how the events map and what it measured against the Silero plugin on the same audio. In short: against the Silero plugin's defaults the end of speech comes about 380 ms sooner, but most of that is the shorter silence setting (0.25 s instead of 0.55 s), which Silero can be given too. At the same setting RealtimeVAD's end is 65 to 110 ms earlier, and LiveKit's turn detector starts 95 to 180 ms earlier. Inside a LiveKit session the turn was committed about 150 ms sooner than with Silero's defaults and about 70 ms sooner than with Silero at 0.25 s.

Measured on 3,279 turns from a live voice assistant, each with its trailing silence, with default settings. Silero's decisions are computed from the very same frame probabilities, so both see identical input. "Speech-off" is RealtimeVAD's last pause before the turn ended, against the first frame of Silero's final run below its threshold.

RealtimeVAD speech-off earlier than … median p25 – p75 p90 earlier in Silero, probability below 0.5 (its default threshold) 100 ms 80 – 150 ms 214 ms 98 % Silero, probability below 0.35 (VADIterator's end threshold) 110 ms 90 – 176 ms 230 ms 98 % Silero VADIterator end, default 100 ms minimum silence 206 ms 186 – 272 ms 336 ms 99 %
Speech-off signals followed by more speech per second of speech turns without any RealtimeVAD pause 1.5 17 % Silero, probability below 0.5 0.14 86 %

Until 0.0.4 the first row read 110 ms. The 10 ms went into not cutting quiet speakers, see the next section.

The end event, against the end Silero's own silence count gives with the same thresholds and the same 0.24 s (2,323 turns where both closed the same segments inside the recording):

RealtimeVAD end earlier than Silero alone earlier in median p25 – p75 later in 0.0.5 82 % 70 ms 40 – 92 ms 0 the same without restarting the count after a click 51 % 18 ms 0 – 76 ms 0

Up to 0.0.4 a single loud 10 ms block inside the quiet after a word (a click, a lip smack, a breath) stopped the quiet count for good and left the end to Silero. That happened in a third of 680 sampled turns. The count now starts again after it.

Reproduce with your own recordings (16 kHz mono WAVs, one turn each, with trailing silence):

python benchmarks/speech_off_lead.py <wav dir> out.json

Up to 0.0.4, "quiet" had a fixed floor (quiet_rms, about −54 dBFS). For a speaker around −32 dBFS that is fine. For a quiet one (a phone line recorded at source level, a distant microphone) the floor sits only a few dB under the speech, their soft word endings counted as silence, and 0.24 s later the segment ended while they were still talking. Since 0.0.5 the floor follows the speaker: it is quiet_rms or 20 dB below the speaker's own level, whichever is lower (floor_margin_db).

The same 3,401 turns, attenuated and sent through a simulated phone line (300–3400 Hz, 8 kHz, μ-law, line noise). "Ended while talking" counts turns with an end that the same detector does not make at the recorded level and that is followed by more speech. "Silero alone" is the same VAD with the quiet clock off, on the same audio.

Speech level Ended while talking: 0.0.4 0.0.5 Silero alone Lost ≥ 100 ms of speech: 0.0.4 0.0.5 Silero alone Speech-off lead 0.0.5 −32 dBFS (as recorded) – – – 0 0 0 100 ms −38 dBFS 361 (11 %) 36 58 13 8 8 108 ms −42 dBFS 609 (18 %) 37 97 26 10 10 116 ms −52 dBFS 1,473 (43 %) 215 155 868 26 23 132 ms −62 dBFS 1,832 (54 %) 269 303 1,778 419 415 124 ms −47 dBFS in room noise at −62 dBFS 746 (22 %) 125 312 295 93 93 0 ms phone line, −38 dBFS 285 416 391 266 234 229 112 ms phone line, −48 dBFS 667 265 275 311 301 294 0 ms

What this says, and what it doesn't:

Quiet speakers are no longer cut. Ends while the speaker talks and lost speech are now where Silero alone has them. In all of these runs RealtimeVAD's last end was never later than Silero's. A noisy quiet line has no lead. When the noise is less than about 20 dB below the speaker (the room-noise row, and the quiet phone line with its line noise), nothing can be called quiet without calling soft speech quiet. RealtimeVAD then ends where Silero does: correct, and no faster. Very quiet and narrowband speech is a Silero limit. At −62 dBFS, and on the phone line, Silero itself is unsure. Speech it never scores 0.9 used to start no segment at all (476 of the phone-line turns, 1,264 at −62 dBFS). The soft start halves that (186 and 380); Silero at its own 0.5 threshold still hears more (139 and 353). More turns found also means more ends counted in the phone rows. Amplifying such input before the VAD helps Silero most. Borderline endings. Ends with speech of the original recording inside the 0.24 s that counted as quiet are rarer than in 0.0.4 by a factor of 10 at −52 dBFS (1,970 turns then, 182 now), but restarting the count after a click added some back (141 without it). Ends followed by more speech and lost speech did not rise with it. The phone path is simulated, and the reference for "still talking" is the original wideband recording. One speaker, one microphone.

What to set:

If … then your input is quiet and clean nothing; the lead stays you would rather keep the old fixed floor VAD(floor_margin_db=None) soft starts open segments you don't want (background voices) VAD(soft_start_s=None) you want Silero's own count only, no early end VAD(quiet_rms=0) your input is quiet or a phone line, and clean try VAD(normalize_to_dbfs=-30), see below
python benchmarks/quiet_input.py <wav dir> out.json

Silero is less sure about quiet speech, most of all on a phone line: it finds fewer turns and drops out inside them. VAD(normalize_to_dbfs=-30) amplifies the frames Silero sees, by up to 20 dB and never into clipping, until speech sits at −30 dBFS. Levels, the quiet clock and the audio you get back use the input as it came. Same turns as above:

Speech level No segment at all: off on Lost ≥ 100 ms of speech: off on −32 dBFS (as recorded) 0 0 0 2 −52 dBFS 138 127 26 5 −62 dBFS 380 357 419 40 −47 dBFS in room noise 220 215 93 21 phone line, −38 dBFS 186 142 234 125 phone line, −48 dBFS 542 499 301 265 phone line, −58 dBFS 1,569 1,203 910 411

It is off by default because it is not free at normal level: 2 of 3,401 turns lost more than 100 ms, speech-off was earlier than Silero in 96 % instead of 98 % of turns, and in one phone-line turn the end came later than Silero alone. It needs Silero to score the speech 0.5 at least once before it acts, so the first quiet words of a stream can still be missed. On noisy quiet input the ends moved by more than the benchmark's "ended while talking" count can judge, so that count is not given here; borderline endings did not rise.

"mm-hmm", "yeah", "okay": 200 real ones from meeting recordings (AMI corpus, close microphone, 0.15–0.8 s long). Up to 0.0.4, 50 of them were not reported as speech at all: Silero scored 35 between 0.5 and 0.9, below the start threshold, and 15 below 0.5. With the soft start 25 are missed, 15 of them Silero's own. A start comes a median 160 ms after the word begins. Whether such a sound is a backchannel, a turn or an interruption is not a VAD question and not answered here.

The numbers come from one speaker and one capture chain: browser capture with noise suppression and echo cancellation, mostly quiet rooms. The lead needs audio that actually goes quiet after a word, and noise suppression helps that. In the 137 noisier turns (room level above −70 dBFS) the median lead was 102–124 ms. Without noise suppression in a loud room, expect less; with noise within about 20 dB of the speaker, none. Earlier is not the same as correct: at the recorded level, whether a speech-off sometimes lands inside a soft word ending was not checked against word timings. The quiet-input table above checks it against the same audio at normal level. The 100 ms are for speech-off. end waits 0.24 s after speech-off in both cases; its own gain over Silero is smaller (a median 70 ms, none in 18 % of turns) and depends on the noise. Whisper is mostly not detected (Silero scores it below 0.5). Laughter, coughs and sneezes often are. A DC offset in the input hides the silence from the quiet clock: no early end then, nothing lost. 16 kHz mono only. pip install -e ".[dev]" pytest

The edge-case tests in tests/audio/ run on about 100 MB of freely licensed audio that is not in git (speech in 8 languages, noise, music, coughs and laughter, whisper, real backchannels and hesitations). Without it they are skipped. To get it (about 1.3 GB of downloads, checked by sha256):

python tests/audio/fetch_audio.py python tests/audio/fetch_backchannels.py pytest tests/audio

They take about 10 s with 8 worker processes and print what each test guards, with the measured value and its limit. Sources and licenses: LICENSES-audio.md, LICENSES-backchannels.md.

MIT. The bundled speech model is Silero VAD (MIT).

entry.title: Chinese frontier AI models carry the fingerprint of export-controlled GPUs
entry.content:
Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs Executive Summary

Our forensic analysis of publicly released AI models finds evidence that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models. Six models released by these companies since April 2026 contain numerical patterns matching Blackwell hardware, whereas earlier models from the same companies match NVIDIA’s older Hopper generation. The findings suggest that several leading Chinese AI developers have begun using Blackwell to train their newest models. U.S. officials and press reports had already alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips, without publishing technical evidence.

The evidence comes entirely from the models’ own published weights, rather than from leaks or insider accounts. We recover traces of the models’ initial values, and then search for the hardware configurations and initial configurations that reproduce them; for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3, we also confirmed the match on physical Blackwell chips. The fingerprint identifies how the weights were created and supports, without proving, the inference that Blackwell also performed the training. Specially configured AMD hardware, which is also restricted from export to China, is the only alternative we have identified; we have excluded it for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and consider it very unlikely for the other five models. Notably, our findings provide technical evidence of access to advanced computing hardware, but do not establish where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated.

Table 1. Hardware fingerprints in successive models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group Link ↗

Lab Model Released Chip the model was started on DeepSeek DeepSeek-V3 Dec 2024 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) DeepSeek-V4-Flash Apr 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 DeepSeek-V4-Pro Apr 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 Moonshot AI Kimi K2 Jul 2025 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) Kimi K2.5 Jan 2026 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) Kimi K3 Jul 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 Kimi K3.1-Pro Nov 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 MiniMax MiniMax-M2.7 Apr 2026 NVIDIA Hopper MiniMax-M3 Jun 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 Ant Group Ling-3.0-flash Aug 2026 NVIDIA Hopper Ling-3.1-flash Oct 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300

• Requires a U.S. license for export to China; none have been reported.

A Hopper fingerprint cannot distinguish an H800 from an H100 SXM or H200; the H800 identifications above are lab disclosures, not findings of this method.

Full list of models in Appendix 2 ↓

Main Findings Six models from four Chinese labs read as Blackwell-trained. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match NVIDIA’s Blackwell-class B200 or B300 chips, which have 148 processor cores (called streaming multiprocessors, or SMs). DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1-Pro and Ling-3.1-flash match the GB200 or GB300 chips, also Blackwell-class, which have 152 processor cores. Kimi K3.1-Pro starts from the same seed as K3, and may be a checkpoint of K3 with further post-training. Chinese labs started training on Blackwell relatively recently. DeepSeek’s models read as Hopper-trained through DeepSeek-V3 (released in December 2024), and as Blackwell from DeepSeek V4 (released in April 2026). Moonshot’s models read as Hopper through Kimi K2.5 (January 2026) and as Blackwell from K3 (July 2026). One Moonshot model sits in between: Kimi K2.7-Code, posted six weeks before K3, is built on the Hopper-era weights but contains a small part that matches the B200 or B300. MiniMax’s models read as Hopper through M2.7 (April 2026) and as Blackwell from M3 (June 2026). Ant Group’s Ling-3.0-flash (August 2026) reads as Hopper, while its Ling-3.1-flash (October 2026) reads as Blackwell. The Hopper readings do not identify a specific chip: H800s, H100 SXMs and H200s share the same fingerprint. Not every Chinese AI lab has switched to Blackwell. The newest models we could read from Alibaba (Qwen), Zhipu (GLM), Tencent, Xiaomi and StepFun all read as Hopper-trained. Meituan says its LongCat-2.0 was trained entirely on “AI ASIC superpods,” and we found no NVIDIA fingerprint in the model weights it’s released. The method gets known answers right. For 24 specific models, the developer has publicly said what hardware was used. In every case, our method agrees with the public announcement. NVIDIA’s own Nemotron-3 Ultra, whose technical report names the GB200 for one phase of its training, reads as 152 SMs, the same as Kimi K3. The matches are far stronger than chance would explain. Even unrelated numbers can appear to match when enough combinations are tried. Across the roughly 6 trillion seed-and-layout combinations in our search, the strongest chance match would be expected to reach about 8 sigma—a measure of how far a result stands above ordinary random variation. The strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma. Even the weakest individual test we report reaches 20 sigma. The training runs were data-center scale. From each model’s size and the amount of data it was trained on, we estimate that the two largest runs, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, each needed thousands of Blackwell GPUs for two to three months, assuming each model was trained on the hardware that initialized it. Our best estimates are about 4,500 and 3,000, the equivalent of about 11,500 and 7,500 H100s, the previous-generation NVIDIA chip in which AI training clusters are commonly sized, and about 12,000 Blackwell GPUs across the five runs (Table 2). At roughly $70,000 per GPU—the cost implied by a Wall Street Journal report that about 36,000 Blackwell chips being installed in Malaysia for ByteDance’s use would cost more than $2.5 billion—the largest of these clusters would cost roughly $200 million to $300 million, and the five together more than half a billion dollars. These figures cover only the final training runs; the labs’ total spending on export-controlled GPUs is likely in the billions of dollars.

Table 2. Rough scale of each training run Link ↗

Model H100 equivalents Blackwell GPUs, best estimate Blackwell range Estimated run length DeepSeek-V4-Flash 3,500 1,500 250–5,000 50 days DeepSeek-V4-Pro 7,500 3,000 750–6,500 70 days Kimi K3 11,500 4,500 1,000–9,500 70 days MiniMax-M3 3,500 1,500 200–7,000 60 days Ling-3.1-flash 4,000 1,500 400–6,500 100 days All five 30,000 12,000 7,000–22,000

Each estimate is a run’s training compute divided by what one Blackwell GPU delivers over the run, rounded to the nearest 500. Training compute is about six operations per active parameter for every training token, plus attention. We assume the GPUs ran at about 20% of their peak speed, in line with other disclosed Blackwell training runs (25% for DeepSeek, which has reported 39% for its previous model), and for the run lengths shown, which we estimate from release timelines. H100 equivalents convert at NVIDIA’s published peak speeds: a B200 or B300 equals about 2.3 H100s, and a GB200 or GB300 about 2.5.

We are not confident in these estimates. They rest on assumptions that the weights cannot confirm: how efficiently each lab used its GPUs (often called MFU), which no lab has published for these runs; how many tokens each model was trained on (DeepSeek’s counts are its own, and we take them on trust; the others are our estimates, made from the weights by a method we have not yet published); how long each run lasted, which no lab has stated; and that training stayed on the hardware that created the weights. Run length matters most, because halving it doubles the GPU count. Two disclosed runs on the same hardware show the spread: Mistral says it trained Mistral Large 4, which has the same number of active parameters as DeepSeek-V4-Pro, on 3,800 Grace Blackwell GPUs, while Microsoft says it trained MAI-Base-2, a model of similar size trained on more data, on 16,000 in 38 days. At that pace the two largest runs here would have needed about 8,000 to 9,000 Blackwell GPUs. The figures cover only the final training run of each model, not experiments, earlier runs or serving.

Revised November 12, 2026. The first version of this report gave 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs for the largest runs and $150 million to $200 million for the largest cluster. Those figures assumed the GPUs ran as efficiently as NVIDIA’s own benchmarks, and training runs disclosed on Blackwell have been less efficient. The estimates above replace them. We have also added H100 equivalents and estimated run lengths.

Our investigation

A model’s weights, also called parameters, are the billions of adjustable numbers that determine how it processes information and produces answers. Training repeatedly adjusts these numbers; but before training can begin, they need initial values. In the software examined here, those values come from a pseudorandom number generation (PRNG) algorithm called Philox: Philox produces seemingly random numbers in a deterministic way. The starting input for Philox is a number called the “seed.” Given the same seed and settings, Philox produces the same numbers every time. This lets engineers repeat an experiment from the same starting point.

To fill billions of weights quickly, PyTorch, the software framework used in the development of most major AI models, divides the work that Philox does among many parallel workers on the GPU, called threads. (It does this through cuRAND, NVIDIA’s library for random number generation.) Each thread generates its own sequence of numbers from the seed and fills a particular set of positions. The number of threads then determines how those positions are shared out. On the NVIDIA chips examined here, a sufficiently large initialization uses the maximum of 2,048 threads for each processing unit, called a streaming multiprocessor (SM). A chip with more SMs therefore assigns the same job to more workers, changing where their numbers go.

Figure 1 illustrates how this works on a simplified GPU with six SMs and eight threads per SM, giving 48 threads in total. Imagine the weights as a long row of empty boxes, wrapped into a grid to fit on the page. The first thread fills the first box, the second fills the second box, and so on through all 48 threads. The first thread’s next number then goes into box 49, its next into box 97, and so forth. The black outlines follow this one thread through the grid: the first thread fills every 48th position. The colors identify which processing unit supplies each set of values, while the brightness in the right-hand panel represents the value itself.

Now keep the seed fixed, but use a GPU with five SMs instead of six. In our simplified example, that means 40 threads rather than 48. The first thread generates exactly the same sequence, but now puts its numbers in boxes 1, 41, 81, and so on, rather than boxes 1, 49, 97. Figure 2 follows these numbers as their positions change. Across the grid, only 6 percent of the values match the original arrangement. The seed is right, but the worker count is wrong. That is what makes the arrangement of model weights a clue to the chip used to create it.

Reproducing the weights therefore requires two things to be right at once. The seed must generate the right numbers, and the thread count must put them in the right places. A correct seed with the wrong thread count mostly gives the right numbers in the wrong positions; a correct thread count with the wrong seed gives different numbers. Figure 3 shows why only the correct combination recreates the original arrangement.

On real chips, the thread counts are much larger, but the principle is the same. In the NVIDIA configurations examined here, the Hopper H100 SXM, H200 and H800 have 132 SMs and use 270,336 threads; the Blackwell B200/B300 have 148 SMs and use 303,104 threads; and the Blackwell GB200/GB300 have 152 SMs and use 311,296 threads. Recovering the thread count therefore tells us which of these hardware groups matches the starting arrangement, although it cannot distinguish chips within a group. A Hopper match, for example, cannot tell an H800 from an H100 or H200.

The question is whether enough of that arrangement survives training for us to recover it. Some weights, such as those reserved for words or symbols never encountered during training, can remain untouched and retain their starting values almost exactly. We can compare these preserved values directly with the starting values generated by a candidate seed and thread count. Figure 4 shows such a comparison: DeepSeek-V3’s preserved weights match the Hopper arrangement, while DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s match the Blackwell arrangement.

Even weights that training has changed can retain a faint trace of their starting values. Each final weight is its starting value plus all the adjustments made during training. If those adjustments do not completely cancel or overwhelm the starting differences, some of those differences survive. For example, two weights that begin at 0.2 and 0.8 and each increase by about 0.1 will still be ordered the same way afterward. Real adjustments vary much more, so one weight tells us little. But across hundreds of thousands of weights, we can test whether higher starting values still tend to correspond to higher final values. Figure 5 shows this weak but measurable relationship. It is a finding in these weights, not a property guaranteed to survive every training run.

These surviving traces let us work backward. Suppose, in an invented example using Figure 1’s layout, seed 7 makes the first thread produce 0.2, −0.5 and 0.8. With 48 threads, those values go into positions 1, 49 and 97; with 40 threads, they go into positions 1, 41 and 81. If the published weights preserve the first pattern, we can try candidate seeds and thread counts until we recreate it. In the actual investigation, we compare thousands of values in their corresponding positions. Untouched weights can match exactly; trained weights may show only the weaker resemblance described above. In either case, we look for the combination that best reproduces the surviving pattern.

We then test that combination on weights we kept out of the search. Having chosen a seed and thread count using one set of weights, we use them to predict the starting values of a different set, without changing either setting to improve the fit. A match on these previously unused weights is stronger evidence than a match confined to the weights that helped us choose the combination. Figure 6 shows the comparisons: DeepSeek-V3 matches the initialization layout of Hopper H100 SXM, H200 or H800 chips; DeepSeek-V4-Flash matches Blackwell B200/B300; and Kimi K3 matches Blackwell GB200/GB300.

In our investigations, we found patterns strongly suggestive of initialization on Blackwell chips in six models from four Chinese companies: DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro from DeepSeek, Kimi K3 and Kimi K3.1-Pro from Moonshot AI, MiniMax-M3 from MiniMax, and Ling-3.1-flash from Ant Group. V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match the 148-SM layout; the other four match the 152-SM layout. These are fingerprints of the starting weights, which support, but do not by themselves prove, the use of Blackwell chips for training AI models.

Limits of our investigation

Notably, the forensic method we used to identify the hardware on which these models were initialized only works for certain models. It needs published weights, so closed models cannot be checked. It also needs a recognizable, hardware-dependent pattern from the software that generated the starting weights. PyTorch on the GPUs examined here leaves such a pattern; Baidu’s PaddlePaddle framework, which was used to train Baidu’s ERNIE-5.5 model, does not. We were able to recover the seed for ERNIE-5.5 (2760), but could not identify which hardware was used to initialize it. Likewise, weights initialized on an ordinary processor rather than a GPU leave no GPU fingerprint; several of Alibaba’s Qwen3 models were initialized this way, and thus leave no trace of which GPUs were used to train them. We also found no fingerprint in Meituan’s LongCat-2.0, which the company says was trained on “AI ASIC superpods,” or in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, despite an exhaustive search.

The method identifies the hardware that generated the starting weights, not every chip that later helped train the model. When a training run creates its weights on the same GPUs that will train it, the fingerprint points to both. But a lab could generate the weights on one system and move them to another, or continue training an existing model on new hardware. The weights alone cannot rule out those possibilities. A mixed cluster introduces the same limitation. If NVIDIA chips generated some weights and Huawei chips later helped train them, the NVIDIA pattern could survive without revealing Huawei’s participation. Different NVIDIA generations could leave different patterns in the parts they initialized, if those traces survived. In Kimi K3, at least 64 separately seeded processes each left the same 152-SM layout. A Blackwell-compatible pattern therefore supports its use at initialization, subject to the AMD alternative below; it does not establish that the entire training run used Blackwell. A Hopper pattern likewise does not rule out later training on Blackwell.

The weights also cannot reveal who owned the chips or where they were located. Blackwell systems can be rented from data centers outside China. The evidence concerns access to the hardware; by itself, it does not establish that chips were smuggled into China or that an export-control violation occurred.

Could a different chip produce one of these Blackwell-compatible patterns? Among the NVIDIA configurations tested here, the older chips cannot: software can use fewer of a chip’s processing units, but cannot give it more than it physically has. Under the standard PyTorch behavior examined here, they cannot produce the 148- or 152-SM layouts. The China-market Blackwell graphics cards use a different number of threads per SM and do not produce either total.

AMD presents a different possibility. An MI300X normally uses 304 processing units, but it can be divided into two groups of 152 or configured to use only 148. Its random-number software can also generate the same underlying sequences as NVIDIA’s. Such configurations would be very unusual, but we confirmed on a physical MI300X that, limited to 152 or 148 of its units, it reproduces the layouts we associate with Blackwell, so the layout alone does not settle the question.

To distinguish them, we looked for small numerical differences in the values themselves. AMD and NVIDIA perform one calculation in the number-generating process slightly differently. On a physical MI300X, DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s preserved weights point to NVIDIA: in the 377 values where the two vendors’ results differ, the published weight matches NVIDIA’s in 363 and AMD’s in none. The same test could not settle the other five models, but we consider the AMD explanation very unlikely for them. In its normal configuration, an MI300X produces neither layout; a lab would have had to configure an entire cluster to use the same number of processing units as a Blackwell chip. Other public evidence also points to Blackwell: U.S. officials and press reports have alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips, and Ant Group’s public code includes benchmark results generated on a GB300.

Verifying our findings

To reproduce the result that linked DeepSeek-V3 to Hopper and DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Blackwell, we ran unmodified PyTorch on a Hopper-class NVIDIA H100 and a Blackwell-class NVIDIA B300. We had identified DeepSeek’s seed number as 953049583, and found that it was used in the initialization of both DeepSeek-V3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Using that seed, the H100 reproduced the preserved starting values in DeepSeek-V3, but not V4-Flash; the B300 reproduced the preserved values in V4-Flash, but not V3. On the B300, unmodified PyTorch reproduced 461 of the 469 selected rows in DeepSeek-V4-Flash with correlations above 0.99, including 445 entire rows that matched bit for bit. Eight selected rows were partly changed by training. On the H100, it reproduced all 57,344 preserved values in DeepSeek-V3 bit for bit. Neither chip reproduced the other model’s preserved rows. Changing the seed by one reproduced no matching rows on either machine. On a rented GB200, unmodified PyTorch likewise reproduced all 13 of Kimi K3’s preserved rows using Moonshot’s seed, 20256586; changing the seed by one reproduced none. The code and the preserved weights needed to repeat these checks are public; the same comparison also runs without a GPU.

Our forensic method also gets the right answer when the answer is already known. There are 24 cases where a developer has publicly named the hardware behind a specific model; our forensic method agrees with every one. Meta’s Llama 3.1 models, trained on H100s, read as 132; eight of EleutherAI’s Pythia models, trained on A100s, read as 108. NVIDIA’s own Nemotron-3 Ultra, whose technical report names the GB200 for one phase of training, reads as 152, the same as Kimi K3. DeepSeek and Moonshot have reported H800 use for earlier models. Our Hopper readings are consistent with those disclosures, but would also be consistent with H100 SXM or H200 hardware; they do not independently verify H800 use.

When we compare the published weights with the numbers generated by a candidate seed and chip layout, some resemblance is inevitable even if the candidate is wrong. How much resemblance counts as evidence depends on how many weights we compare: agreement across a handful of numbers could easily be accidental, while agreement across thousands is much harder to explain by chance. Our statistical model accounts for the number of weights compared and measures how far the observed match exceeds the resemblance expected by chance. We express that distance in standard deviations, or sigma. A higher score means stronger evidence against an accidental match, provided the statistical model correctly describes the random variation in the data.

We must also account for how many candidates we tried. Searching roughly six trillion combinations of seed and layout gives us trillions of opportunities to find a lucky match. Under a normal-distribution model, a positive match of five sigma or more occurs by chance about once in 3.5 million comparisons. That would be striking in a single test, but unsurprising somewhere in a search as large as ours. We therefore use approximately eight sigma as our benchmark for assessing accidental matches across the full search.

Our findings exceed that benchmark by a wide margin. We first select a seed and layout using one set of weights, and then test that same combination on a separate set that played no part in choosing it. This checks whether the apparent fingerprint extends beyond the numbers that led us to it. The strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma; even the weakest individual test reported reaches 20 sigma. Under our statistical model, these results are far too strong to attribute to accidental resemblance. They establish evidence of a shared initialization pattern; identifying precisely which computing hardware produced that pattern, and whether it also performed the training, requires the separate arguments discussed above.

Conclusion

Based on our forensic investigation, we believe that we have strong evidence that six Chinese AI models were initialized on export-controlled NVIDIA hardware, and that for DeepSeek-V4-Flash the evidence is conclusive; we believe that this initialization also strongly suggests that they trained on the same export-controlled hardware. While this leaves unanswered other questions—such as the circumstances through which the companies that developed these models acquired export-controlled NVIDIA systems—we believe that this fact deserves urgent attention from the public.

entry.title: Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer
entry.content:
Today, we're open-sourcing Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B, together with our unified inference framework and deployment tools. Edge0-145B is the world's first open-source on-device AI model with 145 billion parameters. It brings coding, reasoning, and agent capabilities that rival frontier cloud models to your own computer.

On-device AI has long forced a tradeoff between model capability and what the hardware can run. Larger models demand more memory, bandwidth, and power; smaller models can struggle with complex work. Moving that work to the cloud adds model-provider fees, data-handling constraints, and a dependence on connectivity.

This release addresses those constraints in four ways:

The constraint What Edge0-145B makes possible Large models are difficult to run on personal hardware. A 145B model runs locally on a compatible laptop, with reported peak memory of 29GB and decoding above 80 tokens/s. Small on-device models can fall short on demanding tasks. Coding, reasoning, and instruction-following results are competitive with specific frontier cloud models, as the comparisons below show. A useful assistant needs to finish work, not just answer questions. The model plans, writes and runs code, debugs errors, and checks results visually for projects such as 3D scenes, games, hardware programs, and PCB designs. Cloud workflows bring recurring fees, sensitive-data restrictions, and network dependence. Local inference incurs no corresponding cloud-model token or API fees; data can stay on the computer, and core capabilities keep working offline. Hardware and electricity still cost money.

We're releasing the full stack so developers can reproduce the results, evaluate or fine-tune the models, and integrate them into their own products.

Get the model weights, explore the inference framework, or try the Edge0 App.

How We Make 100B+ Parameter AI Run on a Personal Computer Edge0-145B Laptop Performance: Memory, Speed, and Power

Edge0-145B makes a 145-billion-parameter model usable on a personal laptop. A useful local model has to fit in memory, process prompts promptly, generate fast enough to use, and keep power consumption under control. It also needs to sustain longer tasks.

Requirement Reported Edge0-145B result What it enables Memory 29GB peak memory Runs on a compatible personal laptop, such as a MacBook Pro, without a server. Prompt processing 1,100+ tokens/s prefill Processes long prompts, including dozens of pages of code, before generation begins. Generation 80+ tokens/s decode Generates faster than a person reads. Power Approximately 120W typical power Sustains operation without throttling in the reported setup. Long tasks 128K–256K context Maintains essentially the same speed on long inputs, supporting extended work.

Our earlier Edge0-35B phone release reported peak memory below 2.5GB. On an iPhone 18 Pro Max, Edge0-35B delivers 37+ tokens/s using approximately 2.5GB of memory. Edge0-145B has roughly four times as many parameters; its laptop comparison reports 80+ tokens/s and 28GB peak memory. These measurements apply to different models and hardware.

On-device model scale over time. The chart covers 67 open models of at least 1B parameters from 14 labs, intended for phones, laptops, and AI PCs. Same-size base, instruct, and reasoning variants count once; each line tracks a lab's largest model, including releases before July 2025. Filled points mark new highs and hollow points other releases. The scale is logarithmic below 40B and linear above it. Apple is excluded because its weights are not released. Sources: vendor announcements and model cards.

Why On-Device Models Have Stayed Small

Memory limits kept most on-device models below 10B parameters before September 2026. Apple Intelligence's on-device foundation model had approximately 3B parameters, while Google's Gemini Nano came in 1.8B and 3.25B versions. Even a 7B model could consume approximately 4GB of memory.

Larger models faced a memory wall. Model weights occupy storage and must be read during generation, competing for limited memory and bandwidth with the operating system and other apps. Even an aggressively compressed 35B model could need approximately 20GB of memory, far more than a phone could make available.

Compute, bandwidth, and power created competing constraints. Larger models offered more capability, but strained memory capacity, generation speed, and battery life. Making models smaller helped them fit, often at the cost of capability.

Privacy alone could not close that gap. Apple Intelligence protected user data, but Apple acknowledged that its on-device model was not designed for agentic applications requiring general world knowledge. The prevailing assumption was that on-device intelligence could not match the cloud.

Under the Hood of Edge0: Four Layers of Model and Inference Design

We designed Edge0-145B and its inference engine together to reduce the memory and data movement that make large models difficult to run locally. The design spans architecture, training, loading, and scheduling.

Architecture: share large matrices across sparse experts. Sharing matrices substantially reduces the weights that must be stored and moved while keeping the expert count unchanged. Each group of 64 experts shares two large matrices, while each expert retains a small set of parameters that captures its differences. Previously, every expert stored a complete set of matrices. Of the model's 145B total parameters, only approximately 10B participate in computation on each inference step.

Training: build for local execution from day one. We train the model in its on-device architecture from the outset, with deployment constraints built into its design. This avoids treating local deployment as a compression or pruning step after training a cloud model.

Loading: pipeline GPU memory, system memory, and SSD access. Reading and computation overlap across three storage tiers, avoiding serial waits. Frequently used “hot experts” remain in GPU memory. An expert library of approximately 40GB sits in system memory, with experts brought into GPU memory as needed. Approximately 48GB of vocabulary data resides on the SSD and is read on demand.

Scheduling: use the CPU and GPU together. The GPU computes cached experts while the CPU handles the remaining work in parallel. Speculative decoding verifies multiple candidate tokens at once, spreading the cost of reading weights across more output tokens. These choices support the reported 80+ tokens/s decode rate.

Model and inference-engine design work together to make 100B+ parameter inference practical on personal computers. Source: internal testing.

Together, these changes let parameter counts grow from tens of billions to more than a hundred billion without proportional increases in memory use, power consumption, and latency.

What Edge0 Can Do: Anything From Chat to Complex Work on Your Computer

Edge0-145B can carry a complex task through to a usable result. Its coding and reasoning capabilities support local workflows that combine planning, tool use, execution, debugging, and visual checks. The benchmarks establish its capabilities; the demonstrations show how it puts them to work.

Coding and reasoning that rival frontier cloud models

Edge0-145B is competitive with specific frontier cloud models across coding, reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following:

Coding: It scores 64.6 on DeepSWE 1.1, ahead of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next at 58.7 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 54.4. Reasoning and knowledge: It scores 90.4 on GPQA-Diamond, close to DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 90.8 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 91.3. Instruction following: It scores 80.6 on IFBench, ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 79.2 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 62.5.

Its 86.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 also exceeds Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's 83.3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731's 82.7, and Claude's 78.2. On AA-LCR, Edge0-145B scores 79.3 to Claude's 78.0. These comparisons apply to the named models and evaluations.

The largest gains over Qwen3.8-27B, a mainstream on-device model baseline, are in agent and coding work: 18.5% on Terminal-Bench and 53.1% on DeepSWE. The relative gains on HLE, GPQA, and IFBench are 14.9%, 1.3%, and 1.4%, respectively.

DeepSWE 1.1 and Terminal-Bench 2.1 evaluate agent and coding work. HLE, GPQA-Diamond, and IFBench cover reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following. The complete evaluation setup, hardware environment, and reproduction instructions are being released with our technical report.

Competitive capability with a smaller memory footprint

Edge0-145B combines a 72.8 mean score across six benchmarks with 29GB measured peak memory. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next averages 71.7, with an estimated 70GB footprint for standard 4-bit deployment. That puts Edge0-145B at about 40% of the estimated baseline memory while delivering comparable or higher capability, enabling local use on a 48GB laptop.
